clue.text: Spooner's kept carp somewhere in Kent

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so his version trades the first sounds of a two-word phrase

parts.note: kept is stayed and carp is moan; swapping the first sounds of 'stayed moan' gives this

explanation.surface: Someone in Kent keeps a carp, the fish, perhaps in a garden pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stayed moan' with the opening sounds swapped becomes 'maid stone', spelt MAIDSTONE. 'Carp' looks like the fish but is the verb to grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidstone is the county town of Kent, an English county south-east of London, so the place is located there.

clue.text: Constant piercing buzz arising frequently

indicators.note: in a down clue something arising travels upward, so the letters read from bottom to top
a thing that pierces goes right into another, ending up inside it

parts.note: a buzz is a low hum
C is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

explanation.surface: A persistent buzzing noise keeps coming up again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed hum is split open and the constant goes between MU and H.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Do you go there much?' means often, so the adverb is a synonym used in questions and negatives.

clue.text: Island state having change of direction

indicators.note: one compass point is changed for another, so a single letter is swapped out

parts.note: a state of the USA
north, replacing west (W)

explanation.surface: An island nation goes through a political shift of course.
explanation.walkthrough: IOWA swaps its W (west) for N (north). 'Island state' reads as one phrase, but 'Island' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland, famous for its abbey.

clue.text: Adult bears turned and fled from hot area

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: standard abbreviation for adult
bears, as in carries or has
fled means ran away

explanation.surface: A grown-up surrounded by bears turns and flees a scorching spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal covers both the adult and the verb together, not just one word. 'Bears' looks like animals but is a verb meaning has.
explanation.definitionFit: Saharan describes something belonging to or coming from the Sahara, the great desert of North Africa.

clue.text: Swimmers see coral at sea in which eel disappears

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and all over the place, so the order is jumbled
letters that disappear from a group are taken out of it

parts.note: taken as written
these three letters are the ones removed

explanation.surface: Divers spot coral out at sea, where an eel slips out of view.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking E, E and L out of SEECORAL leaves SCORA, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Killer whales are marine mammals that live in the ocean, so they are things that swim.

clue.text: Maybe painting outside of hotel below eastern embankment

indicators.note: in a down clue the lower piece comes later in the answer

parts.note: standard abbreviation for eastern

indicators.note: something outside of another wraps around it

parts.note: a painting is one example of artwork
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Perhaps a painting hangs outside a hotel, below an eastern bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks a painting as one example of the broader word. In a down clue, 'below' puts the eastern letter on top.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthwork is a bank or mound of soil built up, often as a defence, which is exactly an embankment.

clue.text: Nerd bewitched taking out long novel

indicators.note: something novel is new, so the remaining letters take a fresh order
taking something out removes it from the rest

parts.note: taken as written
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A spellbound geek gives up on a lengthy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: BEWITCHED loses ITCH to leave BEWED, which is rearranged. 'Long novel' reads as a book, but 'long' is a verb and 'novel' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dweeb is American slang for a boring, socially awkward person, close kin to a geek or a nerd.

clue.text: Doctor caught ignoring leader is dismissed

indicators.note: ignoring the leader means leaving out the first letter

parts.note: standard abbreviation for doctor
copped is slang for caught

explanation.surface: A doctor caught out ignoring their boss gets the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copped' is informal British slang for caught, as in 'copped it'. 'Leader' looks like a boss but is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A player dropped from a team has been left out or sacked, the same as being let go from a job.

clue.text: Simple trio following Kay attempt to grab article

parts.note: the three letters after K are L, M and N, spelt out as words

indicators.note: to grab something is to take hold of it, so one piece clutches another

parts.note: an attempt is a try
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Three people try to snatch a newspaper piece after someone called Kay has a go.
explanation.walkthrough: Kay is the letter K spelt out; the trio after it is L, M and N, written as their names EL, EM and EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary means basic and easy to grasp, as in Sherlock Holmes's 'Elementary, my dear Watson'.

clue.text: Support workplace to set up American deal

indicators.note: in a down clue something set up is raised so that it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: short for laboratory, a place of work
standard abbreviation
to deal is to trade

explanation.surface: Someone backs setting up an office to strike an American business deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' looks like a verb in a business story; here it is a noun for a structure.
explanation.definitionFit: A balustrade is a railing held up by small pillars, which supports and guards the edge of stairs or a balcony.

clue.text: Firmly grasp piece of cake

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to fasten tightly or secure a grip on something

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as gripping a slice of cake; the two phrases are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means tighten or secure, as with a belt; as a noun it is an easy task or sure thing.

clue.text: Officer gaining lead from evidential material

indicators.note: gaining something means taking it in, so it ends up inside

parts.note: a corporal is a non-commissioned officer

indicators.note: the lead of a word is the letter at its front

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A police officer gets a tip-off from the forensic evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Officer gaining lead' suggests a detective; 'evidential material' reads as one phrase, but 'material' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means having a physical body, tangible rather than spiritual, which is what material means as an adjective.

clue.text: Rat and other rats sharing small insects

parts.note: a grass is British slang for an informer

indicators.note: two words sharing a letter overlap, so one copy of it is dropped where they meet

parts.note: to shop someone is to inform on them
the letter for small, which both words have

explanation.surface: A rat and its fellow rodents divide up some tiny bugs to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The two informers overlap on their common S. A grass and a shopper are both British slang for someone who betrays others to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasshoppers are jumping plant-eating creatures with six legs, members of the order of insects called Orthoptera.

clue.text: Shows face by accepting award

parts.note: pan is slang for a face, as in deadpan

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so it sits inside

parts.note: by as in multiplication: three by four is three times four
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Someone turns up in person to pick up a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows face' reads as appearing in person, but 'Shows' alone is the definition. Pantomimes are British Christmas stage shows for families.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantomime is a theatrical entertainment, so the plural is a set of stage productions.

clue.text: Mate's do after leaving quiet church

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other in the answer
whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters are removed

parts.note: to do something is to accomplish it
the call for silence
the Church of England

explanation.surface: A friend's party happens once the quiet church service ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a party noun; here it is the verb meaning achieve. The 's is short for 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A mate can be a partner in crime, and an accomplice is someone who helps another commit an offence.

clue.text: Account with little money causing stresses

parts.note: standard abbreviation for account
cents are small coins

explanation.surface: A bank account with hardly any funds is a source of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stresses' looks like worry; it is the emphasis on a syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is the emphasis placed on a syllable in speech, so the plural noun matches stresses.

clue.text: Starfleet vying occasionally with alien security measure

indicators.note: occasionally means every now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of the two words
the film's extraterrestrial

explanation.surface: A Star Trek fleet competing with an alien race now and then takes precautions.
explanation.walkthrough: The every-other-letter run spans both words, and ET then completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety net is literally a net to catch falling performers, and figuratively any backup protection against failure.

clue.text: Senior citizen remains in East London terrace

indicators.note: Cockney speech of East London drops the H sound at the start of words

parts.note: an offer that remains open still holds
Ter. is the street-name abbreviation for terrace

explanation.surface: A pensioner stays on in a row of houses in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, from London's East End, famously drop their H's, so HOLDS becomes 'OLDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldster is an informal word for an elderly person, the counterpart of youngster.

clue.text: Coastal town's broadcast picked up

indicators.note: something picked up is heard, as by a radio receiver

parts.note: to put something on air is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A seaside town's radio transmission is received.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayr is a seaside town on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayr sits on the Firth of Clyde, so it is a town by the sea on the Scottish shore.

clue.text: Extremely powerful hit by two females surged in popularity

parts.note: too means excessively
a knockout is a blow strong enough to floor someone
F twice, the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A massive chart hit by two women became hugely popular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely powerful hit' reads as a big song; it splits into extremely and a knockout punch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that took off suddenly became successful or fashionable, as a plane rises sharply into the air.

clue.text: Top cycling finish

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round from one end to the other like a wheel turning

parts.note: to play out a game is to finish it

explanation.surface: A first-rate bike race ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top cycling' suggests a sporting champion; the PLAY at the front of PLAYOUT moves to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To top a rival is to beat them, and to outplay someone is to perform better than them in a game.

clue.text: Sort wine for relatives

parts.note: a sort is a kind
red wine

explanation.surface: Picking out a bottle of wine for the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a verb meaning choose; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindred is a collective word for family members and blood kin, one's relations taken together.

clue.text: Guns behind fortification screens are most similar

indicators.note: to screen is to shield from view, so one piece is hidden inside

parts.note: a gun nest is a fortified emplacement for guns
taken as written

explanation.surface: Weapons concealed behind defensive walls are as close as can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is the hidden piece. A machine-gun nest is guns behind a fortification.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearest can mean closest in resemblance, as in the nearest thing to a match, so it equals most alike.

clue.text: Engineer that made poor toy

indicators.note: to engineer something is to construct or contrive it, so the letters are built into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Blaming the engineer who produced a shoddy plaything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like a person; it is the verb that rearranges the twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Potato Head is a plastic children's plaything, a potato figure with attachable eyes, ears and mouth.

clue.text: Last of bunch refuse to leave with urgency

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

indicators.note: whatever is to leave goes away, so it is removed

parts.note: refuse is rubbish or waste
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: The last people in a group decline to go anywhere in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb; it is the noun meaning rubbish, and it loses its W.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is speed driven by pressure of time, the same hurried need that urgency names.

clue.text: Cat traverses this plain in entertainment show

indicators.note: whatever a thing traverses lies within its span, so taking that spanning thing away leaves what it crossed

parts.note: a cabaret is a nightclub entertainment
these letters, split around the middle, are the ones taken away

explanation.surface: A cat walks across this flat grassland during a variety show.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: the answer is what the cat spans inside the show. 'This plain' looks like open country but is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare means without decoration or addition, just as plain describes something simple and unadorned.

clue.text: Maybe Burgundy's covering cored vegetable

indicators.note: coring removes the centre, so the middle letter is taken out

parts.note: a beret is the classic French hat, and Burgundy is a French region

explanation.surface: A burgundy-coloured wrapping, perhaps, around a hollowed-out vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks Burgundy as one example of a French place, where a beret might be worn. 'Burgundy' also hints at the beetroot colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Beet is the root crop grown for sugar or eaten as beetroot, a common garden vegetable.

clue.text: Principal ways mothers used to keep under control

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
kept in line means kept under control

explanation.surface: The chief methods mums once relied on to keep children disciplined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to' looks like the past tense; it belongs to the container signal, with mothers holding the phrase for under control.
explanation.definitionFit: Main lines are the chief railway routes, so they are the principal ways or routes of travel.

clue.text: Meal canteen regularly supplied is delight

indicators.note: something supplied at regular intervals comes every other step, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the even-numbered letters of both words

explanation.surface: Food served by the works canteen at regular intervals is a joy.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts with the second letter of 'Meal' and carries on through 'canteen'; taking only 'canteen' leaves too few letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate someone is to make them very happy, so the verb is a synonym of delight.

clue.text: Run-down employee's third to quit quickly

indicators.note: whatever quits goes away, so it is removed

parts.note: speedy means quick

indicators.note: the third of a word is the letter in position three

parts.note: the third letter of the word

explanation.surface: A worn-out worker's third job to be quickly abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: SPEEDY loses its P to leave the answer. 'Quickly' is an adverb but must stand for an adjective here, a common setter's licence.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy describes a shabby, neglected place, so it matches the adjective for something dilapidated and in poor condition.

clue.text: Conduct of deviant state minister is twice ignored

indicators.note: deviant means departing from the norm, so the letters stray from their order
something ignored twice is left out on two occasions, so those letters go two times over

parts.note: taken as written
these two letters are removed, twice

explanation.surface: The behaviour of a rogue government minister is overlooked twice.
explanation.walkthrough: Two copies of IS go, one I and one S from each word. 'Conduct' looks like behaviour; it means handling.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatment is the way someone or something is handled, and conduct as a noun can mean management or handling.
